args.Message: ---**SPECIAL TESTS KNEE JOINT** ---**I TESTS FOR LIGAMENT INTEGRITY** ---**A COLLATERAL LIGAMENTS** ---**1 VALGUS STRESS TEST** PURPOSE To assess the integrity of the medial collateral ligament MCL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Knee is slightly flexed approximately 20 30 to unlock the joint • Stabilize the lateral aspect of the knee • Apply a valgus force to the lower leg while stabilizing the thigh POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive medial joint opening compared with the opposite side • Pain along the medial knee INDICATES MCL injury/insufficiency ---**2 VARUS STRESS TEST** PURPOSE To assess the integrity of the lateral collateral ligament LCL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Knee is slightly flexed approximately 20 30 • Stabilize the medial aspect of the knee • Apply a varus force to the lower leg POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive lateral joint opening • Pain along the lateral knee INDICATES LCL injury/insufficiency ---**B CRUCIATE LIGAMENTS** ---**3 LACHMAN TEST** PURPOSE To assess the integrity of the anterior cruciate ligament ACL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Knee flexed approximately 20 30 • Stabilize the femur with one hand • Hold the proximal tibia with the other hand • Pull the tibia anteriorly POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive anterior translation of tibia • Soft/absent firm end feel compared with the normal side INDICATES ACL injury/tear Very important Lachman is generally more sensitive for ACL injury than the anterior drawer test particularly in the acute knee ---**4 ANTERIOR DRAWER TEST** PURPOSE To assess the ACL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Hip flexed and knee flexed to 90 • Stabilize the foot • Grasp the proximal tibia with both hands • Pull the tibia anteriorly POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive anterior movement of the tibia compared with the opposite side INDICATES ACL injury/insufficiency ---**5 POSTERIOR DRAWER TEST** PURPOSE To assess the integrity of the posterior cruciate ligament PCL PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Knee flexed to approximately 90 • Stabilize the foot • Place both hands around the proximal tibia • Push the tibia posteriorly POSITIVE SIGN • Excessive posterior translation of the tibia INDICATES PCL injury/insufficiency ---**II TESTS FOR MENISCAL INJURY** ---**6 MCMURRAYS TEST** PURPOSE To assess for medial and lateral meniscal lesions PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine • Fully flex the knee • For medial meniscus externally rotate the tibia and apply valgus stress while extending the knee • For lateral meniscus internally rotate the tibia and apply varus stress while extending the knee • Palpate the joint line POSITIVE SIGN • Pain • Palpable/audible click or clunk at the joint line INDICATES Possible meniscal tear ---**7 APLEYS COMPRESSION DISTRACTION TEST** PURPOSE To differentiate meniscal pathology from ligament pathology PROCEDURE Compression • Patient lies prone • Knee flexed to 90 • Stabilize the thigh • Apply downward compression through the heel • Rotate the tibia internally and externally Distraction • Maintain the same position • Apply traction to the tibia while rotating it POSITIVE SIGN Compression positive • Pain reproduced with compression/rotation Suggests meniscal pathology Distraction positive • Pain reproduced with traction/rotation Suggests ligament/capsular pathology ---**III JOINT EFFUSION PATELLOFEMORAL DYSFUNCTION** ---**8 FLUCTUATION TEST** PURPOSE To detect knee joint effusion particularly larger effusions PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine with the knee relaxed/extended • Examiner compresses the fluid from one side of the knee toward the opposite side • Observe/palpate for a fluid wave POSITIVE SIGN • A palpable/visible fluid wave or fluctuation INDICATES Knee joint effusion ---**9 PATELLAR TAP TEST** PURPOSE To detect knee joint effusion PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine with knee extended • Gently press/compress the suprapatellar region to move fluid beneath the patella • Tap the patella downward against the femur POSITIVE SIGN • Patella rebounds/floats and taps the femur producing a palpable tap INDICATES Significant knee joint effusion ---**10 CLARKES TEST / PATELLAR GRIND TEST** PURPOSE To assess patellofemoral dysfunction particularly chondromalacia/patellofemoral pain PROCEDURE • Patient lies supine with the knee extended • Examiner places the hand proximal to the patella • Apply gentle downward pressure to the patella • Ask the patient to contract the quadriceps POSITIVE SIGN • Pain behind/around the patella • Inability to maintain quadriceps contraction because of pain INDICATES Possible patellofemoral dysfunction/chondral pathology ---**IV OTHER MEASUREMENT** ---**11 Q ANGLE** PURPOSE To assess patellofemoral alignment and the lateral pull on the patella MEASUREMENT Q angle is formed by the intersection of • Line 1 ASIS centre of patella • Line 2 centre of patella tibial tubercle PROCEDURE • Patient positioned with the knee in the appropriate standardized position • Identify and mark • ASIS • Centre of patella • Tibial tubercle • Use a goniometer to measure the angle between the two lines POSITIVE/ABNORMAL FINDING An increased Q angle may indicate increased lateral patellar alignment/pull and may be associated with patellofemoral dysfunction INDICATES • Patellofemoral malalignment • Predisposition to lateral patellar tracking/instability
